Supermarkets across Europe have been hit by a suspected cyber-attack affecting their fridges and freezers, and raising concern about the vulnerabilities of internet-connected hardware from industrial machinery to humble domestic appliances.

Smart devices which are connected to the internet can include fridges, central heating, and even washing machines.

And while that makes them easier to control remotely, in theory, any device which goes online can potentially be exploited by malicious actors.

However, that doesn't mean hackers can easily take control of it, and big brands generally go to great lengths to make sure their tech is secure.

Exploits have been found before in some devices. In 2015, researchers demonstrated how a vulnerability in a Samsung smart fridge could allow them to intercept internet traffic.

But there's no evidence domestic appliances are being targeted in the cyber-attacks which targeted supermarkets in November.

Ciaran Martin, former chief executive of the UK's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) says manufacturers needed to do more to make connected devices secure.

"There's a lot more that we need to demand of big tech to give us safer devices and products in the first place," he said.

He advised consumers to keep devices updated and enable multi-factor authentication wherever possible.

"I know it's a pain, but it only takes a few seconds," he said.

Since April 2024, UK law has required manufacturers of certain consumer smart devices to meet minimum cyber security standards, including requirements around passwords and security updates.

The NCSC said it was working with international partners and industry to understand the supermarket incidents, but it was unaware of any impact on the UK.

However, researchers from UK Cyber Defence have identified more than 800 refrigeration and building-control interfaces associated with British retailers that can be accessed over the public internet.

That doesn't necessarily mean they can be hacked, but it could leave them exposed to attackers exploiting weak passwords or software vulnerabilities.

The government has already held talks with senior food retailers about cyber resilience, following earlier attacks on supermarkets.

Helen Dickinson, chief executive of the British Retail Consortium, has said cyber incidents are a major concern for retailers, with businesses working alongside the NCSC to share intelligence and strengthen their defences.

It would not be the first time that hacks have raised concern about impact on food supply.

When UK supermarkets M&S and the Co-op were targeted by ransomware hackers in May 2025, the retailers struggled to stock some shop shelves with fresh deliveries.

Customers across the UK complained of empty shelves in the days following the attack.

Tom Hegel, a researcher at cyber-security firm SentinelOne, said retailers must be clearer about responsibility.

"The question retailers need to answer is who owns the security of that equipment, not just who repairs it," he said.

He said internet connectivity can make everyday technology more convenient, but security needed to keep pace.

"Once an attacker can operate those controls, legitimate functions such as defrosting become tools for disruption," he said.

"Changing a setting can destroy physical stock, not just interrupt a computer system."

Outside of the home, connected tech is used to remotely manage industrial machinery and vehicles.

Cyber security expert Ken Munro pointed to a 2015 demonstration in which researchers remotely hacked a Jeep through its internet-connected entertainment system, prompting improvements in vehicle security.

"Fortunately, the vehicle industry woke up to this and fixed the problem," he said.

Mobile connections are also widely used to monitor equipment in power plants and water networks, allowing engineers to manage systems remotely.

Munro said UK utilities were generally good at securing these connections, but standards varied around the world.

His biggest concern was smaller, poorly funded utility companies which may still be relying on older, vulnerable equipment.

Without proper protections, "any factory or equipment" connected to the internet - ranging from carmakers to electricity or transport infrastructure - could face similar risks, said Olivier Daloy, a cybersecurity expert at Zscaler.

Umuryango uharanira iterambere ry’umugore wo mu cyaro, Réseau des Femmes Oeuvrant pour le Développement Rural , wizihije imyaka 40 umaze ushinzwe, uvuga ko wishimira uruhare wagize mu guteza imbere uburezi bw’umwana w’umukobwa, bufatwa nk’urufunguzo rw’iterambere n’andi mahirwe mu buzima.

Uyu muryango washinzwe mu 1986 n’abagore bari bahuriye ku ntego yo guharanira uburenganzira n’iterambere ry’abagore, by’umwihariko abo mu cyaro, binyuze mu gukora ubuvugizi ku bibazo bitandukanye byababangamiraga.

Mu myaka 40 umaze ukora, Reseau des Femmes uvuga ko wageze kuri byinshi mu byo wari wariyemeje, birimo guteza imbere uburezi bw’umwana w’umukobwa no kuzamura imibereho y’abagore.

Annonciate Mukayitete, Umuyobozi Mukuru wa Reseau des Femmes, yavuze ko igihe uyu muryango watangiraga, umugore yari agifite amahirwe make yo kwiteza imbere mu nzego zitandukanye.

Yavuze ko mu byo bashyizemo imbaraga harimo guteza imbere ubuzima n’uburezi bw’umwana w’umukobwa, kuko ari byo shingiro ry’iterambere rirambye.

Ati: “Kubera ko uburezi ari rwo rufunguzo rw’iterambere iryo ari ryo ryose, iyo umuntu abonye amahirwe yo kwiga, bimufasha gusobanukirwa n’ibindi bintu byinshi birimo ubukungu, ubuzima n’izindi nzego.”

Minisiteri y’Uburinganire n’Iterambere ry’Umuryango (MIGEPROF) yashimye Reseau des Femmes uruhare yagize mu guteza imbere umugore n’umuryango muri rusange.

Umunyamabanga Uhoraho muri iyi Minisiteri, Mireille Batamuriza, yavuze ko mu myaka 40 ishize, uyu muryango wagize uruhare mu guhindura imyumvire y’imiryango ku bijyanye no gufatanya imirimo yo mu rugo, ndetse no kwigisha abaturage akamaro ko kwiteganyiriza.

Ati: “Iyo miryango yose ntiwayibara mu myaka 40, kandi ni uruhare rwiza rwabo tubashimira.”

Yasabye Reseau des Femmes gukomeza gufatanya na Leta mu gushakira ibisubizo ibibazo bikibangamiye umuryango.

Ati: “Ni yo mpamvu ubufatanye bwacu ari ngombwa cyane, tugakomeza kuba mu ruhererekane rw’abakora mu gice cyo guteza imbere umuryango.”

Batamuriza yavuze ko batazahwema gukorana n’uyu muryango, by’umwihariko mu bikorwa bigamije kubaka urubyiruko rufite indangagaciro nziza, rutishora mu ngeso zirimo ubusinzi n’ubusambanyi.

Ku rundi ruhande, Reseau des Femmes ivuga ko mu byo yishimira ko yagezeho harimo no guteza imbere ubuzima bw’imyororokere, by’umwihariko ku bana b’abakobwa, ibinyujije mu kubahugura no kubafasha kumenya uburenganzira bwabo kuri ubwo buzima.

Highlights: Wales beat New Zealand for first time in 73 years

France ended South Africa's 100% record in the Nations Championship with a sensational 21-19 victory over the world champions at the Stade de France on Friday.

Les Bleus' victory ensured they kept their lead in the northern group standings heading into the final round of games, which will all be played on Saturday.

Those matches will decide who plays who in the six play-off finals at Allianz Stadium the following weekend.

England ran in 13 tries as they thrashed Japan 78-15 to close the gap to France to just one point.

Ireland are on the same championship points total as England after recovering from a slow start to overwhelm Fiji 43-15 , but trail their Six Nations rivals on points difference.

France face Argentina in the last round and will be favourites to take their place in the final on Sunday, 29 November, but England and Ireland could pounce if they slip up.

England host New Zealand in their final pool game, while Ireland play South Africa, with both of the southern hemisphere sides seeking to bounce back after surprise defeats.

Scotland are in fourth place in the table - above Wales on points difference only - following a hard-fought 15-12 win over Australia on Sunday.

Wales produced the performance of the championship so far with a historic 35-28 victory over New Zealand at a raucous Principality Stadium.

In arguably the biggest shock in Test rugby since Japan beat South Africa in the 2015 World Cup, Wales defended heroically to claim their first win over the All Blacks since 1953.

New Zealand might have lost for the first time in the new championship but they lead South Africa by one point in the southern hemisphere pool after securing a bonus point.

Argentina are third in the table after claiming the only win of the round for the southern hemisphere when they overcame Italy 19-15.

The Nations Championship pits the northern hemisphere teams who compete in the Six Nations - England, Ireland, Scotland, Wales, France and Italy - against southern hemisphere giants South Africa, New Zealand, Australia and Argentina, plus invited sides Fiji and Japan.

All teams will play each of the six in the opposing hemisphere once, with three rounds of fixtures staged in July and another three in November.

Their results will rank the teams within their own hemisphere, from one to six.

On the final weekend in November, there is a three-day play-off event staged at Allianz Stadium in Twickenham. The sixth-placed team in the northern hemisphere plays off against the equivalent in the southern hemisphere standings and so on, culminating in the two top-ranked sides taking each other on.

The winner of that final match is crowned the inaugural Nations Championship winner.

There is also a parallel, Ryder-Cup style hemisphere title. The winner of each of the matches on the play-offs weekend will earn one point for their hemisphere, except for the contest between the two top-ranked teams which delivers two.

The first hemisphere to earn four points over the weekend will be crowned winners.

The Nations Championship trophy and the shield awarded to the best hemisphere are pictured at the Tower of London in London

UPDATED KU WA MBERE 01h13 a.m: Umuvugizi w’Urego rw’Igihugu rw’Ubugenzacyaha, Dr Murangira B Thierry, yemeje ko Umuyobozi w’Akarere ka Gisagara wungirije ushinzwe imibereho myiza y’abaturage, Dusabe Denise na Rangira Anicet, ukuriye Ubugenzacyaha muri kariya Karere (DCI) bafunzwe bakekwaho ibyaha birimo icya ruswa.

Mu nkuru za mbere twabagejejeho zivuga kuri iyi dosiye, twababwiye ko twagerageje kuvugana n’inzego bireba ntibyadushobokera.

Kuri iki Cyumweru tariki ya 01 Ugushyingo 2026, Umuvugizi wa RIB, Dr Murangira B Thierry yabwiye kimwe mu bitangazamakuru byigenga mu Rwanda, ko bariya bayobozi bafunzwe kimwe na Padiri Kayumba Maurice uyobora Paruwasi Gatolika y’i Kansi muri Gisagara.

Uyu Padiri ni we bivugwa ko yatanze ruswa ya miliyoni 4Frw bariya bayobozi bakurikiranyweho.

Ayo mafaranga yayatanze ngo adakurikiranwa ku inyerezwa ry’amafaranga yari agenewe umushinga ugamije kugeza amazi ku Ishuri Ribanza rya Mukomacara, mu Karere ka Gisagara, agera kuri miliyoni 28 Frw byagaragaye ko yaba yaranyerejwe.

RIB ivuga ko yanafunze Nkurunziza Octave, ukekwaho kuba yarabaye umuhuza (komisiyoneri) mu gutanga iriya ruswa.

Dr Murangira avuga ko usibye miliyoni 4Frw ya ruswa abayobozi uw’Ubugenzacyaha muri Gisagara, na Visi Mayor baba barafashe, ngo Visi Mayor Dusabe Denise yagiye yakira amafaranga ya ruswa mu bihe bitandukanye “bikekwa ko ari ayo kugira ngo abikire ibanga Padiri”.

Padiri Kayumba anakekwaho gukora inyandiko mpimbano zigaragaza uburyo amafaranga yari agenewe uriya mushinga yakoreshejwe.

Aba bantu bose uko ari bane bakurikiranyweho ibyaha bibiri, birimo gusaba, kwakira cyangwa gutanga indonke, ndetse no guhimba, guhindura inyandiko cyangwa gukoresha inyandiko mpimbano.

Dr Murangira yatangaje ko Visi Mayor Dusabe Denise na Nkurunziza Octave bafungiye kuri sitasiyo ya RIB ya Kicukiro, mu gihe abandi bafungiye kuri sitasiyo ya RIB ya Remera.

Dosiye zabo ziri gutunganywa kugira ngo zishyikirizwe Ubushinjacyaha.

Amakuru yizewe UMUSEKE wamenye ni uko Dasabe Denise yari yabanje kurekurwa.

INKURU YABANJE YANDITSWE KU WA GATANDATU: Ubushinjacyaha bw’u Rwanda bwarekuye Umuyobozi Wungirije w’Akarere ka Gisagara ushinzwe imibereho myiza y’Abaturage, wari umaze iminsi afunzwe akekwaho icyaha cya ruswa.

Amakuru UMUSEKE wamenye ni uko Dusabe Denise yarekuwe kuri uyu wa Gatandatu arataha nyuma yo gusanga ibyo yakekwagaho bifitanye isano na ruswa ya miliyoani 4Frw byavugwaga ko yafashe ari kumwe n’Ukuriye RIB, mu karere ka Gisagara (DCI), we ntaho ahuriye na byo.

Igenzura ryakozwe ngo ryasanze Dusabe yari asanganywe ubucuti na Paridi bivugwa ko yatswe ruswa, ndetse ngo bari basanzwe bahererekanya amafaranga.

Amakuru UMUSEKE wamenye ni uko ngo Visi Mayor Dusabe ubu wasoje manda y’imyaka itanu, ndetse akaba ari ku rutonde rw’abakandida bashaka imyanya muri Njyanama, haba “hari abashatse kumukururira muri iriya dosiye” kugira ngo atakaze ayo mahirwe yo kuziyamamaza.

Kugeza ubu twagerageje kuvugisha nyirubwite, ariko nomero ye ya telefoni ntabwo iriho.

Ntabwo turabasha kuvugana n’Umuvugizi w’Ubushinjacyaha kuri iki cyemezo urwego rwafashe, niba kinareba Visi Mayor gusa.

Mu nkuru twabajejeho mbere ivuga ku ifungwa rya Visi Mayor, Dusabe Denise n’Umuyobozi wa RIB mu Karere ka Gisagara, Rangira Anicet na bwo inzego bireba zose twaravuganye ntihagira na rumwe rutuvugisha.

Amakuru UMUSEKE twamenye ni uko kiriya kibazo cyagiye kugera mu nzego zo hejuru za RIB, kimaze igihe, aho Padiri wasabwaga gutanga ruswa yabimenyesheje abamukuriye, biza kugera hanze birakurikiranwa.

Ku wa Kabiri w’iki cyumweru tariki 27 Ukwakira 2026 nibwo bariya bayobozi batawe muri yombi nk’uko imboni ya UMUSEKE yakurikiranye iki kibazo yabidutangarije.

Visi Meya Dusabe Denise urangije Manda y’imyaka 5, ari ku rutonde rw’abakandida bahatanira kwiyamamariza umwanya w’abajyanama rusange mu karere ka Gisagara.

Two-year-old Finlay Roberts died after spending hours in a crowded hospital corridor. A coroner raised concerns about a lack of basic observations done by busy staff.

A new early warning system is being introduced in hospital emergency departments in England to help busy NHS staff identify sick children who are dangerously deteriorating.

A high overall score means a child needs more urgent attention. Concerns from staff, parents, carers or the child themselves will trigger an immediate escalation of care.

It comes after Health Secretary Yvette Cooper promised to stop "corridor care" for sick children because of long waits for hospital beds.

The new National Paediatric Early Warning System (PEWS) asks staff to check, log and grade vital signs, such as blood pressure, heart rate and oxygen levels.

The initiative is designed to save lives ahead of winter, when pressure on the NHS is at its highest.

On the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg, Cooper recently talked about the case of two-year-old Finlay Roberts, who died in 2024 after spending hours in a hospital corridor before being discharged.

Cooper apologised to Finlay's parents on behalf of the NHS, saying: "No child should be treated in a corridor. No patient should be treated in a corridor."

Whittington Health NHS Trust, where Finlay waited for treatment, extended its condolences to the family and said it continued to experience periods of exceptional demand across emergency care and, at times, some patients may receive care in temporary clinical areas, including corridors.

A coroner raised concerns about a lack of basic observations done by busy staff , external .

Martha Mills died aged 13 at King's College Hospital in London in 2021

A similar "early warning" system to identify acutely ill adults, including those with sepsis, is already in use in emergency and general NHS hospital wards.

More than 90 hospitals across England have been using the alert system in children's wards, with different age-appropriate assessments available for babies through to teenagers.

The NHS has already said it will expand Martha's Rule to all hospital emergency departments in England. The rule gives patients, families and carers the right to request a rapid review if they are worried that a patient's condition is getting worse and their concerns are not being responded to.

The initiative is named after Martha Mills, who died aged 13 in 2021 after developing blood poisoning, or sepsis, in hospital following a bike accident.

A coroner ruled that her family's concerns about her worsening condition were not listened to and she would probably have survived had she been moved to intensive care earlier.

Martha's parents Merope and Paul came up with the idea of the rule in a bid to change the culture that contributed to her death.

A&E units will have a dedicated phone number that can be called to trigger an urgent review of a patient's care.

Duncan Burton, chief nursing officer for England, said the new early warning system for children in emergency departments was an "important next step in improving care for children and young people across England for this winter - and beyond".

He added: "In fast-paced emergency departments, staff need to spot quickly when a child's condition is deteriorating.

"This standardised approach will help them recognise the warning signs, communicate concerns, and make timely decisions when every moment matters."

The early warning system for children, PEWS, is a collaboration between NHS England and the Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health and the Royal College of Nursing.

Binance customers withdrew $3.6bn (£2.7bn) of assets from the world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange as it reopened on Sunday following what is believed to be the largest hack in history.

The firm suspended all transactions in the wake of the incident, which impacted $6.3bn worth of digital assets.

Major organisations, including the US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), have accused North Korea of being responsible for the cyber-attack .

The company said it has covered around 95% of the assets stolen in the breach but the remaining amount may take longer to source. Binance has repeatedly said it would cover all of the losses linked to the attack.

Binance said on X: "Between 06:00 and 15:30 [GMT] on November 1, we processed $4.649 billion in withdrawals and $1.01 billion in deposits, resulting in a net outflow of approximately $3.64 billion."

There was an "initial spike" in withdrawals, which later declined and "are stabilising as expected", it added.

Sunday's net withdrawals account for just over 2% of the $171bn of assets under its management, said Binance.

The firm said last week that it has reserved more than $6.3bn in funds, to deal with ​the fallout of the attack.

Binance also said withdrawals of more than two dozen major cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin and Ethereum have resumed and that more services will resume in phases once security checks are completed.

Funds linked to the Binance hack continue to be laundered, according to Alec Zebrick, senior manager in global services at Chainalysis, which has been working with the firm and governments to get the stolen money back.

"We continue to see funds being laundered quite actively," he told the BBC's Today Programme.

"The attackers are layering these funds across many thousands of addresses, across thousands of deposits," he added.

AI discovered a massive cyber-security flaw - here's what happened

The attack on Binance has been attributed to TraderTraitor, a North Korean cybercrime group also known as the Lazarus Group, which stole a then-record $1.5bn from crypto exchange Bybit in 2025 .

The FBI on Saturday published a list of cryptocurrency wallet addresses linked to the group and urged partners in the industry to help by blocking transactions involving them.

The exchange scrambled to urge cryptocurrency issuers to freeze affected assets.

Binance said last week that early checks suggest the incident may have started with a compromised laptop that belonged to an engineer, allowing hackers to find a way to make unauthorised transactions.

The hack hit Binance's global centralised exchange, Binance.com, while its US-facing platform has said it was not affected by the issue.

Watch: What we know about Binance's $6.3bn hack and what to do if you're affected

Binance said it had replaced customers' assets using a combination of sources, including its corporate treasury as well as its futures insurance and emergency reserve funds.

"Our commitment remains the same: Binance will fully cover the financial impact of the funds stolen in this incident," the firm said.

Cryptocurrencies are digital assets traded on exchanges such as Binance. Unlike cash, they do not exist in physical form and are managed on computers, smartphones and other digital devices.

Binance was founded in China and has hundreds of millions of registered users globally.

Rusizi: Hari umusore w’imyaka 17 wo mu murenge wa Nyakabuye wari umaze iminsi icumi yarabuze, ashakishwa n’umuryango we, yabonetse mu murenge wa Gitambi yarapfuye.

Amakuru agera ku MUSEKE avuga ko uyu musore witwa Banamwana Dieu Merci, wo mu mudugudu wa Kinunga, mu murenge wa Nyakabuye umubiri we wabonetse mu ishyamba mu gitondo cyo kuri iki cyumweru tariki 01 Ugushyingo 2026, mu mudugudu wa Ruvuruga, mu kagari ka Mashesha, mu murenge wa Gitambi.

Amakuru akomeza avuga ko ku kuwa Gatandatu tarki 31 Ukwakira 2026, inzego z’ubuyobozi zo mu mu murenge avukamo wa Nyakabuye zamenyeshwejwe ibura ry’uyu musore bikozwe n’umuryango we.

Ubuyobozi bw’umurenge wa Gitambi bwahamirije UMUSEKE ko uwo mubiri w’umusore wabonywe n’umukecuru wari ugiye gushaka inkwi mu ishyamba, agatabaza inzego z’ibanze n’iz’umutekano.

Manirarora James Umunyamabanga Nshingwabikorwa w’umurenge wa Gitambi, ati “Ni umubiri w’umusore w’imyaka 17 wabonetse mu gitondo saa moya (07h00 a.m) akaba yitwa Banamwana Dieu Merci. Amakuru y’ibanze yagaragaye ni uko umuryango wari umaze iminsi umushakisha bataramenya aho aherereye.”

Yabwiye UMUSEKE ko uyu musore yari yararangije amashuri abanza ntiyakomeza kwiga ayisumbuye, ikindi ngo amakuru atangwa n’abaturage ndetse n’umuryango we avuga ko nta bikorwa bidasanzwe yari azwimo, bityo ibikekwa byose ku rupfu rwe ngo biracyari mu iperereza.

Ati “Amakuru atangwa n’abaturage ndetse n’ababyeyi be bivugwa ko nta bikorwa bidasanzwe yari azwimo, ibikewa byose biracyari mu iperereza ryatangiye.”

Uyu muyobozi yasabye abaturage gukomeza gutangira amakuru ku gihe, anabibutsa ko nta muturage wemerewe kugaragara mu bikorwa by’ubugizi bwa nabi.

Ku bufatanye bw’izego zitandukanye n’izumutekano, umubiri wa Nyakwigendera wajyanywe mu bitaro bya Mibilizi gukorerwa isuzuma.

Ku wa 2 Ugushyingo(11), isi yizihiza umunsi mpuzamahanga wahariwe guca umuco wo kudahana abakora ibyaha byibasira abanyamakuru.

Uyu munsi washyizweho mu rwego rwo kwibuka abanyamakuru babiri ba Radio mpuzamahanga y'abafaransa (RFI), Ghislaine Dupont na Claude Verlon, biciwe muri Mali ku wa 2 Ugushyingo(11), 2013.

N'ubwo hashize imyaka 13 ibyo bibaye, ishami ry'umuryango w'abibumbye ryita ku burezi, ubumenyi n'umuco (UNESCO) rivuga ko ikibazo cy'ibyaha bikorerwa abanyamakuru gikomeje gutera inkeke ku isi.

Kwicwa, gukubitwa, iterabwoba no gutoteza abanyamakuru biracyakorwa kenshi, nyamara abenshi mu babigizemo uruhare ntibagezwa imbere y'ubutabera nk'uko UNESCO ibisobanura.

Mu mwaka wa 2013, inteko rusange y'umuryango w'abibumbye yemeje umwanzuro ugamije kurwanya umuco wo kudahana abakora ibyaha byibasira abanyamakuru, isaba ibihugu byose gushyiraho ingamba zifatika zo kubikumira no kubikurikirana.

Nk'uko imibare y'ikigo cya UNESCO gikurikirana abanyamakuru bishwe ibigaragaza, hagati ya 2006 na 2024 abanyamakuru barenga 1,700 barishwe, hirya no hino ku isi.

Muri izo mpfu, inyinshi ntizigeze zikurikiranwa ngo abaziguyemo bahabwe ubutabera.

UNESCO ivuga ko kudahana abakora ibi byaha, bituma hakomeza kubaho ubundi bwicanyi, kandi akenshi bikaba ikimenyetso cy'amakimbirane akomeje gukaza umurego mu bihugu bimwe na bimwe, bitewe n'inzego z'ubutabera zidakora neza.

Uyu muryango kandi uvuga ko uwo muco wangiza umuryango mugari, kuko kudahana uwakoze icyaha ari uguhonyora uburenganzira bwa muntu ku butabera.

UNESCO irahamagarira guverinoma, imiryango itari iya leta, ibitangazamakuru n'abaharanira iyubahirizwa ry'amategeko kwifatanya mu rugamba rwo guca burundu kudahana abahohotera abanyamakuru mu buryo bumwe cyangwa ubundi.

UNESCO ivuga ko ku rwego rw'isi, 85% by'ubwicanyi bukorerwa abanyamakuru badahabwa ubutabera. Kuri uyu munsi, UNESCO irasaba ibihugu byose gukora ibishoboka kugira ngo ibyaha bikorerwa abanyamakuru bikorweho iperereza ryimbitse, ababigizemo uruhare bamenyekane kandi bahanwe.

Uyu muryango ushimangira ko kurengera umutekano w'abanyamakuru ari imwe mu nkingi z'ingenzi zo kurinda ubwisanzure bw'itangazamakuru n'uburenganzira bw'abaturage bwo kubona amakuru.

Cyril Ramphosa, South Africa's president, has denied any wrongdoing

A court in South Africa has found a man guilty of stealing more than $580,000 (£432,000) in cash from a farm owned by South African President Cyril Ramaphosa, in a case that mired the head of state in an impeachment saga.

Imanuwela David was found guilty of theft on Monday, as well as conspiracy to commit housebreaking with intent to steal at Phala Phala farm in the Limpopo province in 2020.

Froliana Joseph, a cleaner at the property, was also found guilty of conspiracy to commit housebreaking with intent to steal.

Her brother, Ndilinasho Joseph, was acquitted on all charges.

David was accused of breaking into the cattle farm in February 2020 and taking the cash from a sofa on the property. David then went on a spending spree, buying a range of cars including three Mercedes - among them one for his girlfriend - a Porsche, two Volkswagens as well as diamond-encrusted Rolex watches and a house.

David told the court he had made the money through businesses including diamonds and Bitcoin, claims the court rejected. The court also found that David was the only one of the two convicted who had any of the stolen cash in his bank account.

Pre-sentencing will take place on 13 November.

There have been many twists and turns in what is known as the Farmgate scandal.

The theft was largely unknown until 2022 when it was brought to light by Arthur Fraser, South Africa's former intelligence chief and an ally for the former president Jacob Zuma, when he claimed that Ramaphosa hid the theft from the police and tax authorities.

Ramaphosa admitted the theft took place but denied any wrongdoing.

An independent panel that same year found Ramaphosa could have questions to answer over the burglary. MPs voted against establishing an impeachment inquiry.

In May this year, the constitutional court ruled that parliament had acted unlawfully by shelving the panel's report, and in July Ramaphosa blocked the parliamentary inquiry through a provincial court.

Uganda first deployed its troops to Somalia in 2007

Uganda has begun withdrawing its troops from Somalia after nearly two decades of military involvement in the country.

Uganda's acting army spokesperson Chris Magezi on Monday said the first group of troops deployed to Somalia through a bilateral arrangement had already arrived back home and others would follow in a few days' time.

He said all forces, including those under the African Union (AU) mission, would exit by the end of 2027 in the phased withdrawal.

Uganda was the first African country to deploy troops to Somalia under the African Union Mission in Somalia (Amisom), established in 2007 to help protect the country's transitional government from attacks by Islamist militants.

A first contingent of 109 Uganda People's Defence Forces (UPDF) troops reportedly left the capital, Mogadishu, on Friday, following an announcement by Uganda's army chief, Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba.

Last week, Kainerugaba said Uganda had begun pulling out its troops and would hand over security responsibilities to Somali forces.

"As we promised, we have started withdrawing UPDF from Somalia. After 20 years of a lot of blood and sacrifice, we are handing over security to our Somali brothers," he wrote on X.

On Monday, Magezi said this would mark the end of Uganda's operations in the Horn of Africa country, with Somalia expected to "assume full responsibility for security".

The withdrawal comes after Somalia President Sheikh Mohamud met his Ugandan counterpart Yoweri Museveni in Kampala last week.

The meeting was planned to discuss Somalia's security situation, as well as trade and economic ties between the two countries.

The Somali president reportedly sought to persuade Uganda to extend its military presence.

In remarks during the visit, Museveni urged Somali leaders and citizens to unite in the fight against the militant insurgency led by al-Shabab, which is part of al-Qaeda.

An estimated 4,500 troops are in Somalia under the Africa Union mission, alongside about 2,000 deployed through bilateral arrangements.

Somalia has been battling a prolonged and deadly insurgency for more than two decades.

After Ugandan forces were first deployed to the country in 2007, they played a key role in driving al-Shabab out of Mogadishu and other major towns.

They fought alongside the Somali National Army to recapture strategic territory and secure key government installations.

Ugandan troops were involved in successive Africa Union missions, including the African Union Transition Mission in Somalia (Atmis), which began with the aim of gradually transferring security responsibilities to Somalia.

This was replaced in 2025 by the African Union Support and Stabilisation Mission in Somalia (Aussom), which is focused on strengthening Somalia's security institutions and preparing its forces to take full responsibility for the country's security.

Aussom now faces uncertainty over its future funding, amid plans to wind down US and UN support.

A 12-month transition plan is due to begin in January, giving Somalia and the AU time to seek alternative sources of funding.

President Félix Tshisekedi’s latest remarks on the FDLR raise serious questions about the DRC’s commitment to the Washington Peace Agreement.

During an exchange with the Congolese diaspora in Russia on October 30, Tshisekedi said his government is regrouping FDLR members in Kitona, apparently preparing to transfer them to another country.

This raises a fundamental question, why is Kinshasa negotiating the relocation of the FDLR instead of fulfilling its commitment to neutralize the group?

The Washington Peace Agreement is not a relocation arrangement. It requires concrete security measures to address the threat the FDLR poses. Moving some of its members from one location to another, or transferring them to another country’s territory, does not dismantle the organization, eliminate its military capabilities, or address its genocidal ideology. It merely shifts the problem elsewhere.

The contradictions within the Congolese leadership make the situation even more troubling.

Just two days before Tshisekedi’s remarks, Foreign Minister Thérèse Kayikwamba Wagner told RT that the DRC could not neutralize the FDLR because its members were operating in territories controlled by M23.

Government spokesperson Patrick Muyaya has repeatedly offered similar explanations whenever Kinshasa is questioned about its failure to act.

Yet the president is now telling the world that his government has regrouped FDLR members in Kitona.

So which version should the international community believe? If the FDLR are inaccessible because they operate in M23-controlled territories, how has Kinshasa managed to regroup them in Kitona? And if the government can assemble them in a designated location, what prevents it from proceeding with their disarmament and neutralization?

The FDLR cannot disappear from government statements on Monday, be reported in FRN-controlled areas on Tuesday, reappear in Kitona on Wednesday, and suddenly become another country’s responsibility on Thursday. Kinshasa owes the international community a consistent explanation.

Perhaps the biggest contradiction lies in Tshisekedi’s own political narrative. He repeatedly accuses Rwanda of using the FDLR as a pretext for its security concerns and involvement in eastern DRC. He has even complained that the United States is pressuring his government to neutralize the group.

But if the FDLR is merely a pretext, as Tshisekedi claims, why resist the very action that would remove that pretext? How does one relocate a pretext, and why complain about international pressure to dismantle an armed group you already committed in writing to neutralizing?

The FDLR is not an imaginary organization. Its origins, genocidal ideology, and continued activities in eastern DRC are well-documented. Neutralizing it is not a favor to Rwanda; it is a security obligation and an essential step toward lasting regional stability.

The United States played a central role in facilitating the Washington Agreement. Its credibility now depends on ensuring that commitments made by the signatories translate into measurable action.

Tshisekedi cannot sign an agreement requiring FDLR neutralization, complain about pressure to implement it, and then present relocation as an alternative.

Washington must demand answers; How many, if any, FDLR members are in Kitona? Have they been disarmed? What happens to their command structures and military networks? Under what framework does Kinshasa intend to transfer them abroad?

The question is no longer what Kinshasa is expected to do, but whether it has the political will to do it. And how long will Washington continue turning a blind eye to this failure?

President Kagame Paul speaking during the panel session

ST JOHN’S, ANTIGUA AND BARBUDA – President Paul Kagame says international investors need to rethink their perception of developing economies, arguing that investment risks are not exclusive to poorer countries and should not keep capital away from viable projects.

Speaking at a Commonwealth leaders’ panel in Antigua and Barbuda on Monday, November 2, Kagame said the belief that investments in the Global South carry greater risks than those in the Global North has persisted for too long.

“There is a perception out there that the developing countries […] in making these investments, there are higher risks for the investments in the south than in the north,” he said.

“But it is not true. There are risks everywhere for any investments you want to make.”

Kagame said governments and investors should focus on managing those risks through cooperation and by making resources available to projects with sound commercial prospects.

He said the Commonwealth could help change the way international investors view developing economies, particularly countries that need foreign capital to create jobs, equip young people with skills and expand their economies.

The Rwandan leader returned to the question of investment later in the discussion, when the moderator, Professor Justin Robinson, asked how a small Commonwealth country could attract financing for profitable projects in renewable energy, digital platforms and agro-processing.

Kagame said the size of a country should not determine whether a viable project gets financing. Governments and private investors, he said, should work together to close funding and infrastructure gaps that prevent good projects from taking off.

He also pointed to regional market integration as a way of making investments in smaller economies more attractive.

“It’s not just a small project in a small country, but rather a viable project in a growing market beyond the place where it is,” he said.

He added that governments must put in place policies and strong institutions that connect the public and private sectors.

The moderator used Rwanda as an example of a country that has overcome some of the disadvantages associated with geography. He noted that the country has no coastline or oil resources but recorded 9.4% economic growth in 2025.

Kagame’s remarks come as many developing countries compete for investment while facing higher borrowing costs, limited access to international capital markets and perceptions of political and economic risk.

His message was that investors should assess the commercial prospects of individual projects rather than dismissing opportunities because of the countries in which they are located.

The panel also featured Jamaican Prime Minister Andrew Holness and Samoa’s Deputy Prime Minister Mulipola Anaroso Ismilio.

Holness focused on the cost of government bureaucracy, saying inefficient institutions can hold back development even when financing is available. He called for governments to use technology and artificial intelligence to improve public service delivery.

Ismilio, meanwhile, highlighted the importance of trust, relationships and collective responsibility among Commonwealth countries.

The discussion formed part of the 2026 Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting in Antigua and Barbuda, November 1 – 4, 2026.

MN202611_1fotdva6n4k.t:
The 38th Meeting of the Parties to the Protocol (MOP38), which opened on November 2, 2026.

KIGALI – Ten years after countries adopted the Kigali Amendment to the Montreal Protocol on substances that deplete the Ozone layer, governments are back in Kigali to review and strengthen implementation of the agreement and address outstanding challenges.

At the 38th Meeting of the Parties to the Protocol (MOP38), which opened on November 2, one of the most consequential decisions was how much money to provide developing countries through the treaty’s multilateral fund for 2027–2029.

The Environmental Investigation Agency (EIA) estimates that funding requirements for the three-year period could range from $1.23 billion to $1.692 billion under its principal scenarios.

It recommends a replenishment comparable to the record $965 million provided for 2024–2026. These are independent estimates, not figures agreed by governments

The replenishment will determine the resources available to phase down hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs), transition to alternative cooling technologies, improve energy efficiency and strengthen the systems needed to enforce the agreement.

Meg Seki, the Executive Secretary at the Ozone Secretariat said the next phase must preserve the institutional capacity that has made the Montreal Protocol effective while responding to new demands.

“Our objective should not be to do less with less, but to work smarter, preserve what works well and ensure that the Montreal Protocol remains effective and responsive to future challenges,” Seki said.

The treaty has already overseen the phase-out of 99.5 per cent of ozone-depleting substances globally, with the ozone layer on a path to recovery. The Kigali Amendment adds another demanding task of reducing the climate impact of the gases used in refrigeration and air conditioning.

Rwanda’s Minister of Environment, Dr Bernadette Arakwiye.

Adopted in October 2016, the Kigali Amendment commits countries to reduce HFC consumption by 80 per cent by 2047. Although HFCs do not deplete the ozone layer, they are powerful greenhouse gases.

Full implementation is projected to prevent up to 0.5°C of global warming by 2100. Combined with improvements in cooling energy efficiency, the climate benefit could approach 1°C, according to the EIA briefing.

But the agreement’s success also depends on whether governments can account accurately for the gases being produced, imported and used.

Concerns have been raised about a discrepancy between reported HFC-23 emissions and estimates derived from atmospheric monitoring, calling for better estimation, reporting and monitoring.

Rwanda’s Minister of Environment, Dr Bernadette Arakwiye, said international commitments would achieve little without national systems capable of translating them into practical changes.

“Signals only matter when they are backed by clear rules. Licensing systems, quotas, standards and technician training as essential tools for implementation.,” she said.

Dr Arakwiye also emphasized the need for coordination between environmental and energy authorities, arguing that the transition must link climate protection with energy efficiency and access to sustainable cooling.

“Rwanda wants the tenth anniversary to renew political commitment to the agreement, including through support for the Kigali +10 Declaration and the integration of its objectives into national plans,” she noted.

The funding negotiations will help determine whether developing countries can strengthen enforcement, train their workforce and expand access to cooling without locking themselves into technologies that carry a high climate cost.

Ten years after the agreement was reached in Kigali, the test is whether the promise made in Rwanda can be felt in the farms, hospitals, cold rooms and workshops that depend on cooling every day.

These negotiations come as demand for cooling continues to grow, particularly in developing countries where refrigeration is essential to food preservation, healthcare and business but access to reliable cold-chain infrastructure remains limited.

For African economies, refrigeration is not simply an environmental concern, it is part of the infrastructure needed to reduce agricultural losses, preserve medicines and support industries.

Madi Sakandé, President of the Union of Associations of African Actors in Refrigeration and Air Conditioning (U3ARC) said that inadequate cold storage leaves African countries losing food that could otherwise support local markets and industries.

“When we are importing food from other countries, the industries producing it generate emissions, while we waste our own food. This is the economic cost of failing to expand cooling infrastructure,” Sakandé said.

Anita Gikundiro, Director of Operations at the Africa Centre of Excellence for Sustainable Cooling and Cold-Chain (ACES).

According to experts, the expansion must happen alongside a transition to refrigerants with lower climate impacts, more efficient equipment and better management of gases throughout their lifecycle.

That requires more than purchasing new equipment. Some alternative refrigerants are flammable or operate under high pressure, making technician training, safety standards and appropriate handling essential.

Anita Gikundiro, Director of Operations at the Africa Centre of Excellence for Sustainable Cooling and Cold-Chain (ACES), made the same point from the perspective of the people expected to deliver the transition.

“Targets are written in conference halls. They are made in workshops, in cold rooms, on rooftops and in hospital plant rooms. The Kigali Amendment will succeed in our hands or it will not succeed at all,” she said.

Her observation highlights why investment in skills and infrastructure is central to the agreement. Without technicians who can install, maintain and safely handle alternative refrigerants, countries risk having ambitious policies that do not translate into changes on the ground.

MN202611_1cfaxl26rok.t:
The new rules have been issued by Finance Minister Yusuf Murangwa and Justice Minister Dr Emmanuel Ugirashebuja

KIGALI – Public servants in Rwanda whose actions or failure to act result in the loss of government money or property will be required to repay the losses within 30 days, under new regulations governing public finance management.

The rules, issued by Finance Minister Yusuf Murangwa and Justice Minister Emmanuel Ugirashebuja, make public employees financially responsible for losses attributed to their actions or omissions.

Under the new Ministerial Order No 010/26/10/TC, published in the Official Gazette on October 30, an employee found responsible for a loss must receive a written notice from the head of their institution, stating the amount involved and demanding payment within 30 days.

Payment may also be made in reasonable instalments.

Employees who fail to pay could face legal proceedings before a competent judicial authority to recover the money.

The regulations cover central government institutions, local government entities and non-commercial public institutions, among other public bodies.

The order requires public servants to immediately report any suspected loss of public money or property to their direct supervisors. Reports must also be sent to the official responsible for asset management and the institution’s chief budget manager.

Every reported incident must be investigated, regardless of how it was brought to the institution’s attention.

Where a loss may involve a criminal offence, the matter must be reported to the relevant investigative authorities.

An employee who disputes responsibility may have the matter referred to the courts for determination and possible recovery of the funds.

However, the regulations allow certain losses to be written off where they result from unavoidable circumstances or cannot be recovered following a thorough investigation.

The order also introduces a provision for emergency government spending through what it describes as an “impromptu” budget line.

The provision creates a reserve for urgent and unforeseen expenditure that was not included in the original budget.

At central government level, the reserve will be managed by the Ministry of Finance and Economic Planning. Ministries facing unexpected financial needs can request additional funding, provided they justify the request.

The Finance Minister must approve the allocation and transfer the money to the relevant institution’s budget before it is spent.

Institutions receiving the money will be required to submit quarterly reports explaining how it was used.

Local government entities will also have their own emergency budget provisions, with their respective executive heads authorised to approve spending. They must report quarterly to their councils.

The order does not prescribe a fixed amount or percentage of the national budget for these emergency allocations. Their size will be determined during the annual budget preparation process.

The new regulations also require public institutions to separate financial responsibilities, ensuring that the same employees do not control every stage of budgeting, payments, asset management and accounting.

Every public institution must maintain an internal audit function and an audit committee, while also establishing systems to identify and manage financial risks.

Public assets must be insured against specified risks. Government buildings, for example, must be covered against fire, earthquakes and floods, while movable property must have protection against fire, theft and floods.

The measures come against a background of repeated concerns over the management and recovery of public funds.

In the Auditor General’s report for the financial year ending June 2025, presented to Parliament in May 2026, Rwf1.47 billion was recovered through preventive audits, compared with Rwf9.3 billion in the previous year.

The report also identified Rwf600 million in unlawful expenditure, down from Rwf2.04 billion in 2024.

Separately, the Auditor General has highlighted difficulties recovering money lost through mismanagement and embezzlement.

In one case, 46 cooperatives were found to have misappropriated Rwf455 million in 2025, but only Rwf10 million had been recovered by December that year.

The new order establishes an administrative process through which public institutions can demand repayment from employees responsible for financial losses, alongside existing investigations and criminal proceedings.

It took effect on October 30, the date of its publication in the Official Gazette.

KAMPALA – Uganda has begun withdrawing its troops from Somalia, setting in motion the end of a military deployment that has lasted nearly 20 years, as the African Union mission faces growing uncertainty over its funding and future.

The Uganda People’s Defence Forces (UPDF) said on Monday, November 2, that it had started withdrawing troops deployed under bilateral security arrangements with the Somali government. The operation is expected to be completed within days.

In a statement issued in Kampala, UPDF Acting Director of Defence Public Information, Colonel Chris Magezi, said the first group of troops under the phased withdrawal had already returned to Uganda.

The military also confirmed that all Ugandan forces in Somalia, including those serving under the African Union Support and Stabilization Mission in Somalia (AUSSOM), would be gradually withdrawn by the end of 2027.

“This will mark the end of Uganda’s enduring 20-year peace and stabilization support operations in Somalia, permitting the Somali Armed Forces to assume full responsibility for security in the country,” Magezi said.

The announcement follows a decision by Uganda’s army chief, General Muhoozi Kainerugaba, to end the country’s military deployment in Somalia. On October 29, Kainerugaba announced that Uganda would withdraw its troops, with the full exit expected by August 1, 2027.

The first 109 Ugandan soldiers reportedly left Mogadishu on October 30.

Uganda first deployed troops to Somalia in March 2007 under the African Union Mission in Somalia (AMISOM), becoming the first African country to contribute forces to the operation.

The deployment followed years of instability after the collapse of Somalia’s central government in 1991. The rise of the al-Shabaab militant group created a major security threat, prompting regional and international efforts to support the Somali government.

Ugandan troops played a central role in efforts to secure Mogadishu, protect government institutions and help Somali forces regain control of territory from al-Shabaab. They also took part in operations to clear roads and towns, particularly in the southern regions.

The African Union mission later transitioned into the African Union Transition Mission in Somalia (ATMIS), before AUSSOM took over in January 2025.

Uganda has remained one of the largest troop contributors throughout these operations. Under AUSSOM’s agreed force allocation, Uganda was assigned 4,500 troops. Ethiopia was allocated 2,500, Djibouti 1,520, Kenya 1,410 and Egypt 1,091.

Uganda’s departure will therefore leave the other four countries as the principal military contributors to the mission, although their actual numbers on the ground may differ from the authorised allocations.

The withdrawal comes as AUSSOM faces financial pressure following a US decision to oppose continued United Nations logistical and operational support for the mission.

In July 2026, Washington informed the African Union that it would not support the United Nations Support Office in Somalia beyond December 31, 2026. The office provides essential services to African Union forces, including food, fuel, water, medical support and transportation.

The decision has raised concerns about how the mission will sustain its operations if alternative funding and logistical arrangements are not secured.

Uganda’s withdrawal does not, by itself, mean that all African Union or United Nations personnel will leave Somalia. The remaining AUSSOM contributors are expected to continue their roles, although the mission’s ability to operate will depend partly on the outcome of the funding dispute.

Somalia also hosts foreign forces operating under separate bilateral security arrangements, including Ethiopian and Kenyan troops. Their presence is not automatically affected by Uganda’s withdrawal from AUSSOM.

The transition comes amid continuing concerns about the ability of Somali forces to maintain security as foreign troops leave. Al-Shabaab remains active in parts of the country.

Somali President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud reportedly asked Uganda’s President Yoweri Museveni to delay the withdrawal from some positions in the Lower Shabelle region, including Barawe, Bulo Marer, Qoryoley and Janaale, where Somali forces may face difficulties taking over security responsibilities.

Uganda’s departure will mark a significant change in Somalia’s security arrangements, placing greater responsibility on the Somali Armed Forces after nearly two decades of support from Ugandan troops.

MN202611_gxb1opxwbr.t:
ST. JOHN’S – President Paul Kagame has arrived in St. John’s, Antigua and Barbuda, to attend the 28th Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM 2026), bringing together leaders from 56 member countries to discuss trade, investment and development cooperation.

The four-day summit, running from November 1 to 4, is being held under the theme, “Accelerating Partnerships and Investment for a Prosperous Commonwealth.”

The meeting is expected to focus on strengthening economic partnerships, attracting investment and addressing shared development challenges, including climate change and the economic vulnerabilities facing small island states.

King Charles III, Head of the Commonwealth, is attending alongside Queen Camilla, and is scheduled to host the traditional leaders summit and banquet on Tuesday.

The gathering also brings together government ministers and representatives from business, civil society and youth organisations.

Rwanda is represented at the ministerial level by Foreign Affairs Minister Olivier Jean Patrick Nduhungirehe, who joined other officials for the opening engagements.

Kagame’s participation comes four years after Rwanda hosted the Commonwealth summit in Kigali from June 20 to 25, 2022.

The 2022 meeting, which had been postponed twice because of the COVID-19 pandemic, brought together leaders and representatives from across the organisation under the theme, “Delivering a Common Future: Connecting, Innovating, Transforming.”

Rwanda joined the Commonwealth in 2009, becoming the second country after Mozambique to enter the organisation without having been a former British colony.

The Antigua and Barbuda summit will conclude with a closed-door retreat of heads of government, where leaders are expected to discuss the Commonwealth’s future priorities and adopt a final communiqué.

Meanwhile, President Paul Kagame joined fellow Heads of State and Government, along with other invited guests, on Sunday evening for celebrations marking the 45th anniversary of Antigua and Barbuda’s independence.

KIGALI – GPS tracking technology, widely used by professional football clubs to monitor players’ physical performance, is gaining attention in Rwanda as the national football federation seeks to strengthen the use of sports science in coaching.

The Rwanda Football Federation (FERWAFA) trained about 70 coaches and other football professionals in the technology during a two-day workshop held on October 29 and 30 at the FERWAFA Hotel in Remera.

The technology allows coaches and sports scientists to collect data on players’ movements during training, including distance covered, running speed, sprints and acceleration.

Combined with other performance measurements, the data helps teams assess players’ physical workloads, adjust training intensity and manage fatigue and injury risks.

Several leading clubs and national teams already use such systems. In England, for example, Premier League clubs use wearable GPS devices supplied by companies such as STATSports to monitor players and inform training decisions. The technology has become part of the wider shift towards data-driven performance analysis in professional football.

FIFA, football’s world governing body, has also evaluated electronic performance-tracking systems to assess their accuracy and reliability as their use has expanded across the sport. Such systems can combine satellite positioning with motion sensors and other measurements to give coaches a more detailed picture of players’ physical demands.

In Rwanda, FERWAFA says the workshop was intended to help coaches, fitness specialists and other football professionals better understand how to interpret performance data and apply it to player preparation.

The sessions were facilitated by four experts: Claudio Altieri, the Amavubi national team’s performance specialist; Serge Mwambali, who works on capacity development for the national team; and GPS specialists Theo Le Floch and Andrew Howit.

At the closing ceremony, FERWAFA interim president Claudine Gasarabwe, accompanied by national team coach Stephen Constantine, said more training sessions would be organised in collaboration with other institutions.

Claudio, who organised the workshop, said another session was planned for next year to help physical performance coaches working with clubs across Rwanda develop their skills.

Constantine said participants who benefited from the training could have opportunities to work with Rwanda’s national teams at different levels. He expressed confidence that those who acquired the necessary knowledge would be able to apply it in preparing national team players.

During the workshop, participants learned how GPS devices work, what performance indicators they provide and how coaches can use the information to inform training decisions.

Theo Le Floch and Andrew Howit demonstrated StatSports devices, which are used by football teams internationally. The programme combined classroom instruction with practical exercises on the pitch.

Muvandimwe 12 FC was used to demonstrate how the StatSports system operates in a football setting.

The next step will be to translate the training into routine practice, enabling coaches to use performance data alongside their technical assessments, medical information and observations to improve player development and team preparation.

Battle hardened Kabila-led FRN rebels have put up a multilayered resistance against the Congolese troops as they push them into Uvira City of south Kivu.

By Monday morning the Congolese troops and their allies were dislodged by FRN from Luvungi.

FARDC command have decided to withdraw the Guépard unit, which had been positioned in Luvungi, in the Ruzizi plain.

Government coalition, troops continue to arrive and are concentrating on the hills overlooking Lubarika and Katogota, while the FRN positions continue to be reinforced as well.

Residents in these areas are fleeing towards Kamanyola, others towards Luvungi, fearing a repeat of the December 2025 scenario that led to the fall of Uvira.

According to our source, members of the FARDC Owls unit appeared demoralized and huddled together.

On Sunday (Nov 1) the Owls and Black Snakes units are said to have replaced the Cheetahs units, accused of treason. The latter were disarmed and replaced.

Meanwhile, during the night of November 2, Congolese and Burundian troops once again tried retaking Kuwamabuye and Gipimo.

However, their attempt to recapture these positions once again failed.

The capture of Luvungi could significantly alter the balance of power and facilitate an advance toward Sange, Kiliba, and Uvira, particularly if the forces present on the heights manage to support this push.

Meanwhile, several strategic positions on the mountains overlooking the Ruzizi plain are under the control of FRN Rebels, who are advancing toward Uvira, Baraka, Fizi, Misisi, Lulimba, and Kalemie.

Reading that the Guépard unit has been pulled back from Luvungi, the question that stays with me is how long the FRN can hold that ground once the pressure shifts. Moves like this tend to be temporary, and the civilians caught between Uvira and Luvungi pay for every reversal. Solid reporting on an axis that most English-language outlets barely touch.

MN202611_1j9ch768wds.t:
Rwanda is seeking to strengthen its renewable energy partnerships and accelerate the adoption of solar power as a delegation led by State Minister for Infrastructure Armand Zingiro attends the 9th General Assembly of the International Solar Alliance (ISA) in New Delhi, India.

The Rwandan delegation, which also includes Rwanda’s Ambassador to India, Jacqueline Mukangira, is joining representatives from member countries and international partners at the November 2–5 meeting to discuss ways of expanding access to affordable, reliable and sustainable solar energy.

The General Assembly provides a platform for member countries to review progress in global solar energy development, strengthen international cooperation and explore solutions to challenges affecting the deployment of solar technologies, particularly financing, infrastructure and access to modern energy.

For Rwanda, participation in the meeting presents an opportunity to explore partnerships, attract investment and access technical expertise that could support the country’s renewable energy ambitions.

Such cooperation could help accelerate solar power projects, expand electricity access in underserved communities and reduce reliance on conventional energy sources.

Discussions are also expected to focus on mobilising financial resources for solar projects, encouraging private-sector participation and promoting technology transfer to make renewable energy solutions more accessible and affordable.

The assembly is taking place alongside the Bharat Renewable Energy Summit & Expo 2026 and the 4th International Green Hydrogen Conference, bringing together discussions on solar power, renewable energy technologies and emerging clean-energy solutions.

The parallel events could also provide Rwanda with opportunities to engage investors, technology providers and development partners interested in supporting Africa’s energy transition.

Potential outcomes for Rwanda include new cooperation opportunities, investment prospects, technical partnerships and knowledge-sharing initiatives that could contribute to the country’s efforts to diversify its energy mix and advance sustainable development.

Rwanda’s participation comes as countries increasingly look to renewable energy to address energy security, climate change and the growing demand for electricity driven by economic expansion and industrialisation.

MN202611_eehf84rqk2.t:
Artificial Intelligence Agents are being adopted by Kenya’s Central Bank (CBK) to help in processing payments, fraud detection, credit risk assessment and customer service.

Robert Mudida the CBK Director of Research said on Monday, that despite adoption of AI agents, the bank would maintain human oversight over decisions made using the technology.

“Agentic AI is at the highest level because these agents are being trained to take over critical decisions that are being done by human beings,” said Mudida.

“It has great opportunities but also great dangers, so we are going slowly, but there are opportunities of using agents in areas like payments,” Mudida said.

Kenya’s financial regulator is also exploring more than 300 artificial intelligence applications to improve operational efficiency, including testing a new AI-powered chatbot.

“We are trying to move as fast as possible, but we are very aware of AI governance, which is very important to ensure the security of data,” Mudida noted.

CBK’s Research Department is already using AI for microforecasting in volatile economic conditions and nowcasting to fill data gaps and provide the Monetary Policy Committee with near-real-time information on the state of the economy.

The regulator’s exploration of AI agents comes as financial institutions increasingly use artificial intelligence to support payment processing, fraud detection, credit risk assessment and customer service.

MN202611_1hc63w4shg2.t:
President Paul Kagame has arrived in St. John’s, Antigua and Barbuda, to participate in the 28th Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM 2026), where leaders are expected to explore new investment opportunities, strengthen trade ties and deepen cooperation on development.

The four-day summit, running from November 1 to 4, is being held under the theme “Accelerating Partnerships and Investment for a Prosperous Commonwealth.”

It brings together leaders from 56 member countries to discuss shared economic priorities, climate resilience, innovation and sustainable development.

Kagame’s participation provides Rwanda with an opportunity to strengthen diplomatic relations, promote the country as an investment destination and explore partnerships that could support economic growth, job creation and infrastructure development.

During the summit, Kagame is expected to join fellow leaders in high-level discussions on how Commonwealth countries can use their collective economic potential to attract investment, expand trade and respond to common development challenges.

The programme also includes discussions on the future priorities of the Commonwealth, alongside engagements involving business leaders, investors and development partners.

These meetings could provide Rwanda with opportunities to promote projects and build relationships with potential investors and international partners.

One of the main potential benefits for Rwanda is increased access to investment and markets.

Stronger trade links with Commonwealth countries could help Rwandan businesses explore new export destinations, develop commercial partnerships and attract capital into sectors such as tourism, technology, manufacturing and infrastructure.

The summit’s focus on investment could also support Rwanda’s efforts to mobilise financing for development projects and encourage partnerships between the government and private sector.

However, such benefits will depend on the agreements reached and whether discussions lead to concrete investments.

Climate resilience and sustainable financing are also important to Rwanda, particularly as the country pursues development while addressing climate-related risks.

Cooperation with other Commonwealth members and development partners could help Rwanda access expertise, technology and financing for climate adaptation and sustainable infrastructure.

Youth employment and innovation are further areas of potential cooperation. With Commonwealth countries discussing ways to expand opportunities for young people, Rwanda could benefit from partnerships in digital skills, entrepreneurship, technology and business development.

Rwanda joined the Commonwealth in 2009 and hosted CHOGM in Kigali in June 2022, an event that brought international leaders and delegates to the country and showcased its capacity to host major international gatherings.

The 2026 meeting offers another platform for Rwanda to maintain its engagement with member states, strengthen its international profile and pursue partnerships that advance its economic priorities.

The summit is expected to conclude with leaders discussing the Commonwealth’s future direction and adopting a final communiqué outlining shared priorities.

For Rwanda, the key measure of success will be whether diplomatic engagements translate into tangible outcomes, including new investment, expanded export opportunities, stronger development partnerships and initiatives that create jobs for Rwandans.

Abasirikare 254 bo mu Ngabo za Repubulika ya Santarafurika (FACA) barimo Ofisiye n'andi mapeti basoje amahugurwa y’amezi atandatu y’imyitozo ya gisirikare igenerwa ingabo zo mu Mutwe Udasanzwe (Basic Special Operations Force Training Course), icyiciro cya kabiri cya 2026. Ayo mahugurwa yatanzwe n’abarimu bo mu Ngabo z’u Rwanda (RDF), yaberaga mu Kigo cy’Amahugurwa ya Gisirikare giherereye i Nasho, mu Karere ka Kirehe.

Uyu muhango wo gusoza amahugurwa wayobowe n’Umugaba Mukuru w’Ingabo z’u Rwanda, Gen MK Mubarakh, ari kumwe n’Umugaba Mukuru w’Ingabo za Santarafurika, Gen Zephirin Mamadou. Witabiriwe kandi n’abasirikare bakuru bo ku mpande zombi.

Aya mahugurwa yari agamije kongerera ubushobozi abasirikare ba FACA mu bikorwa bya gisirikare, binyuze mu mahugurwa akomeye, imyitwarire n’ubunyamwuga bikenewe kugira ngo bashobore gukora imirimo yihariye ya gisirikare no guhangana n’imbogamizi ziba mu bihe bigoye by’ibikorwa bya gisirikare.

Yabashishikarije gukomeza kubahiriza amahame y’ubunyamwuga bungukiye muri ayo mahugurwa, gukorera igihugu cyabo babikunze no gukoresha neza ubumenyi bungutse. Yongeye gushimangira ko RDF yiyemeje gusangiza ubunararibonye n’ubumenyi ifite izindi ngabo z’ibihugu bafitanye ubufatanye, mu rwego rwo gukomeza imbaraga zihuriweho zo guteza imbere amahoro, umutekano n’ituze ku mugabane wa Afurika.

Umugaba Mukuru w’Ingabo za Santarafurika, Gen Zephirin Mamadou, yashimiye byimazeyo Guverinoma y’u Rwanda, ubuyobozi bw’Ingabo z’u Rwanda n’abarimu batanze aya mahugurwa, ku bw’ubwitange, ubunyamwuga n’umurava bagaragaje mu gihe cy’amezi atandatu. Yagaragaje ko ubumenyi, ikinyabupfura n’ubushobozi abasirikare be bungukiye muri aya mahugurwa bizabafasha kurushaho kuzuza inshingano zabo neza no kugira uruhare mu kubungabunga umutekano n’ituze muri Repubulika ya Santarafurika.

2LT Christ Ngboundourou, umwe mu basoje aya mahugurwa, yavuze ko yiyemeje gushyira mu bikorwa ubumenyi n’ubushobozi yungukiye mu Rwanda, mu kurinda igihugu cye n’abaturage ba Repubulika ya Santarafurika.

Mu gihe cy’amezi atandatu abahugurwaga bungutse ubumenyi n’ubushobozi buhanitse mu bijyanye n’amayeri akoreshwa ku rugamba. Muri byo harimo kurasa neza hakoreshejwe imbunda nto n’inini, kurwana badakoresheje intwaro, kwambuka imigezi n’ahantu hari amazi, kugendera ku makarita ya gisirikare, ibikorwa bya gisirikare bikorerwa hifashishijwe indege za kajugujugu, ndetse n’ubundi bumenyi bwihariye.

Gusoza aya mahugurwa ni intambwe ikomeye mu kongerera ubushobozi n’ubunyamwuga abasirikare ba Santarafurika, kandi bishimangira ubufatanye burambye mu bya gisirikare hagati y’u Rwanda na Repubulika ya Santarafurika, by’umwihariko mu bijyanye n’amahugurwa ya gisirikare, kongerera ubushobozi inzego z’ingabo no guteza imbere ubunyamwuga.

Intumwa z’Umuryango w’Ingabo ziteguye gutabara mu karere ka Afurika y’Iburasirazuba (Eastern Africa Standby Force – EASF), ziyobowe n’Umuyobozi wawo, Brig Gen Ronald Rwivanga, kuri uyu wa Mbere tariki 02 Ugushyingo 2026, zatangiye igikorwa cy’iminsi itandatu cyo kugenzura ubushobozi u Rwanda rwemeye gutanga muri uwo muryango.

Iki gikorwa kigamije gusuzuma no kugenzura ubushobozi u Rwanda rwemeye gutanga mu nzego z’igisirikare, Polisi n’abasivili, harebwa uburyo ubwo bushobozi buteguwe neza kandi bushobora gushyigikira ibikorwa byo kubungabunga amahoro n’umutekano mu karere igihe cyose bikenewe.

Mu muhango wo gutangiza ku mugaragaro iki gikorwa wabereye ku Cyicaro Gikuru cy’Ingabo z’u Rwanda (RDF), Maj Gen Dr Ephrem Rurangwa, Umugaba ushinzwe Serivice z’Ubuvuzi muri RDF, yakiriye izo ntumwa mu izina ry’Umugaba Mukuru w’Ingabo z’u Rwanda.

Yashimangiye ko ibikorwa nk’ibi byo kugenzura ari ingenzi mu guhindura ibyo ibihugu bigize uyu muryango byiyemeje mo ubushobozi bufatika bushobora koherezwa mu butumwa. Yagaragaje kandi akamaro ko kugira abasirikare n’abandi bakozi bahuguwe neza, bafite ibikoresho bihagije, ku buryo baba biteguye koherezwa mu butumwa igihe cyose bibaye ngombwa.

Brig Gen Ronald Rwivanga, uyobora Umuryango wa EASF, yasobanuye ko iki gikorwa kiri muri gahunda zisanzwe z’uyu muryango zo gusuzuma ubushobozi buri gihugu cyiyemeje gutanga.

Yavuze ko iki gikorwa kigamije kugenzura ubushobozi bw’abasirikare n’ibikoresho byabo, ndetse n’ubushobozi bw’urwego rwa Polisi n’inzego z’abasivili zishyigikira ibikorwa, harimo na Minisiteri y’Ububanyi n’Amahanga.

Brig Gen Rwivanga yagaragaje icyizere ku myiteguro y’u Rwanda, avuga ko adashidikanya ku bushobozi bwarwo bwo kuzuza inshingano rwiyemeje mu rwego rw’uyu muryango w’akarere.

Muri iyi minsi itandatu, intumwa za EASF zizasuzuma ubushobozi u Rwanda rwiyemeje gutanga mu Ngabo zirwanira ku butaka, izirwanira mu kirere n’urwego rw’Ubuvuzi mu Gisirikare, hakazagenzurwa abakozi n’ibikoresho.

Kuri uyu munsi wa mbere, izo ntumwa zasuzumye umutwe w’ingabo zirwanisha ibifaru (Motorised Battalion), umutwe wa Military Police (Military Police Company) n’Ibitaro byo ku rwego rwa kabiri (Level 2 Medical Unit).

Iryo tsinda kandi ryasuzumye ubushobozi u Rwanda rwiyemeje gutanga mu gutabara indembe cyangwa abakomerekeye mu bikorwa bya gisirikare hifashishijwe uburyo bw’indege, harimo kajugujugu yo mu bwoko bwa Mi-17 n’indege yo mu bwoko bwa Caravan.

Biteganyijwe kandi ko izo ntumwa zizagenzura umutwe w’Ingabo zidasanzwe (Special Forces Squadron), umutwe w’Ingabo zirwanira ku butaka (Light Infantry Battalion), ndetse zikanasuzuma ubushobozi u Rwanda rwiyemeje gutanga mu rwego rwa Polisi.

Iki gikorwa cyo kugenzura ni intambwe ikomeye mu kureba niba ubushobozi u Rwanda rwiyemeje gutanga bwujuje ibisabwa n’Umuryango w’Ingabo ziteguye gutabara mu karere ka Afurika y’Iburasirazuba, bugakoreshwa mu butumwa bwo gushyigikira ibikorwa byo kubungabunga amahoro n’umutekano mu karere.

Perezida w’u Rwanda, Paul Kagame, yavuze ko hakenewe guhindura imyumvire ivuga ko gushora imari mu bihugu biri mu nzira y’amajyambere bifite ibyago byinshi kurusha mu bihugu byateye imbere, ashimangira ko ubufatanye hagati ya Leta n’abikorera ndetse no guhuza amasoko byafasha ibyo bihugu gukurura ishoramari no kwihutisha iterambere.

Ibi yabigarutseho mu kiganiro cyabereye mu nama ya 28 y’Abakuru b’Ibihugu na za Guverinoma bigize Umuryango wa Commonwealth (CHOGM 2026), iri kubera muri Antigua na Barbuda.

Muri iki kiganiro cyibanze ku mpinduka zikenewe mu mitekerereze no mu mikorere kugira ngo ibihugu bibashe guhangana n’ibibazo by’iterambere no kubyaza umusaruro amahirwe bihari, Perezida Kagame yari kumwe na Minisitiri w’Intebe wa Jamaica, Andrew Holness, na Minisitiri w’Intebe wungirije wa Samoa, Mulipola Anarosa Ale Molioʻo.

Abayobozi bari bitabiriye iki kiganiro basabwe kugaragaza imyumvire imwe bumva ko ikwiye guhinduka mu buryo ibihugu byabo bikemura ibibazo bikomeye kandi bigakoresha amahirwe ahari.

Perezida Kagame yavuze ko kimwe mu bikwiye guhinduka ari imyumvire ivuga ko ishoramari mu bihugu biri mu nzira y’amajyambere rifite ibyago byinshi kurusha irikorerwa mu bihugu byateye imbere.

Yagize ati: “Hari imyumvire isanzweho ivuga ko ibihugu biri mu nzira y’amajyambere, iyo bishoye imari mu bikorwa by’iterambere, ishoramari ryabyo riba rifite ibyago byinshi kurusha irikorerwa mu bihugu byo mu majyaruguru y’isi”.

Perezida Kagame yagaraje ko iyi myumvire imaze igihe kirekire igaragara. Nyamara, ikaba atari ukuri. Perezida yavuze ko ishoramari rishobora guhura n’ibyago ahantu hose, naho umuntu yaba ahisemo gushora imari hose.

Yasobanuye ko kugira ngo iyo myumvire ihinduke, hakenewe ubufatanye, guhuriza hamwe ubushobozi no gushyiraho uburyo bwo kugabanya ibyago bishobora guhungabanya ishoramari.

Yongeyeho ko Umuryango wa Commonwealth ushobora kugira uruhare mu guhindura iyo myumvire, kugira ngo ibihugu bidakomeza gufatwa nk’ahantu hashobora guteza igihombo ku bashoramari bitewe gusa n’aho biherereye.

Ikindi kibazo cyagarutsweho ni ikivuga uburyo ibihugu bito byakurura ishoramari, umuyobozi w’ikiganiro yatanze urugero rw’u Rwanda, agaragaza ko nubwo rudakora ku nyanja kandi rudafite peteroli, ubukungu bwarwo bwakomeje kwiyongera ku kigero cyo hejuru.

Yabajije Perezida Kagame icyo ibihugu bito bigize Commonwealth byakora kugira ngo bikurure ishoramari, mu gihe abashoramari bashobora kugira impungenge zishingiye ku bunini bw’isoko, ubushobozi bw’igihugu bwo kwishyura imyenda n’ikiguzi cyo kubona igishoro.

Mu gusubiza, Perezida Kagame yavuze ko hakwiye kubanza gusobanurwa uko umushinga uzashyirwa mu bikorwa kandi ushobora kubyara inyungu, kandi hakagaragazwa uburyo utagomba kubuzwa amahirwe n’igihugu uzakorerwamo.

Yashimangiye ko Leta n’abikorera bakwiye gufatanya gushyiraho uburyo bworohereza abashoramari kubona ubushobozi n’ibindi bikenewe kugira ngo babashe gushyira mu bikorwa imishinga yabo.

Perezida Kagame kandi yagaragaje ko guhuza amasoko ari kimwe mu bisubizo byafasha ibihugu bikiri mu nzira y’Amajyambere kwagura amahirwe y’ishoramari.

Yavuze ko umushinga udakwiye gufatwa nk’ugenewe isoko rito ryo mu gihugu kimwe gusa, ahubwo ko ukwiye kureberwa mu rwego rw’isoko rinini kandi rigenda ryaguka, rirenga imbibi z’igihugu urimo.

Yashimangiye ko kugira ngo ibyo bigerweho hakenewe politiki zishyigikira ishoramari, inzego zifite ubushobozi bwo gushyira mu bikorwa inshingano zazo, imiyoborere myiza ndetse n’imikoranire ihamye hagati ya Leta n’abikorera.

Iyi nama ya 28 ya CHOGM 2026 yahurije hamwe Abakuru b’Ibihugu na za Guverinoma 30, ikaba ifite insanganyamatsiko igira iti: “Kwihutisha ubufatanye n’ishoramari bigamije kubaka Commonwealth iteye imbere.”

Kujyeza ubu Umugande Mohamed Iga ukinira ikipe ya EAUR niwe umaze gutsinda amanota menshi kuko amaze gutsinda amanota 71 aho akurikiwe n’umunya Brazil Saymon Feitosa ukinira ikipe ya POLICE VC aho we amaze gutsinda amanota 65.
